overlap.summary: The cloud determines movement while Moses asks Hobab to help with wilderness camping.
overlap.reasoning: Departure timing and local camping knowledge can be complementary. This is a possible contextual reading; the text does not give a complete division of navigation responsibilities.

overlap.title: Moses’ relatives and the in-law label
overlap.summary: KJV calls Hobab Moses’ father-in-law; ASV and WEB call him brother-in-law. Exodus names Reuel and Jethro, while Numbers calls Hobab Reuel’s son. The apparent family conflict depends on the kinship reading.
overlap.reasoning: If every in-law label denotes the same paternal relationship, the named father and son create tension. Reading Hobab as brother-in-law avoids that particular generation conflict; equating Jethro and Reuel as two names for one person is a possible explanation, not an explicit identification in these passages. Numbers’ punctuation alone does not prove which antecedent receives the label.
overlap.scope: This comparison is edition-sensitive. Do not claim all translations make Hobab the father-in-law, or that Kenite and Midianite must be mutually exclusive ethnic identities. No original-language semantic range or family genealogy is established solely from English translations. Alias and clan relationships remain interpretation questions. The Greek of Judges 1:16 names Jethro where the Hebrew and KJV name no one, so in the Greek book both Jethro (1:16) and Hobab (4:11) carry the same in-law word. Brenton’s English renders that Greek word “father-in-law” in both verses; the same Greek word is used for the woman’s father at Judges 19:9, so it does not by itself fix the relationship. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.
